# Correlation Is Not Causation {#sec-causation}

```{python}
#| label: ch13-setup
import textwrap

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.ticker import FixedLocator, ScalarFormatter

from scripts import water as w
from scripts.figures import ACCENT, INK, figsize, grid, is_epub, style
from scripts.prose import alt_text_holds, number_words, spans, text_holds

A = w.A
res = w.res()
k = res["k"]
names, colors = w.names(), w.colors()
kind = {c: n.rsplit(", ", 1)[0] for c, n in names.items()}
rho = res["irca_infant"].set_index("cluster")
bins = res["irca_infant_bins"]
bins = bins[bins["n"] >= 20]
rho_lo, rho_hi = rho["spearman_rho"].min(), rho["spearman_rho"].max()
pooled_rho = rho["all_clusters_rho"].iloc[0]
pooled_n = int(rho["all_clusters_n"].iloc[0])


def sgn(x):
    return f"{x:+.2f}".replace("-", "−")
```

```{python}
#| label: ch13-checks
# Values for the prose, and guards for its sentences whose words depend on the data.
NUM = number_words(zero="no")
WORD = number_words()


IM_YEARS = spans(A.OUTCOME_YEARS["infant_mortality"])
text_holds(IM_YEARS == "2017–2019 and 2021–2023", "the years in the captions of fig-wat-pooled and fig-wat-within")
c_lo, c_hi = int(rho["spearman_rho"].idxmin()), int(rho["spearman_rho"].idxmax())
text_holds(pooled_rho > 0 and rho["spearman_rho"].abs().max() < 0.2
           and abs(rho_hi - pooled_rho) < 0.01, "weak associations, one as large as the pooled one")
cl = res["clusters"]

# @tbl-within-spread: how much four features still vary inside each cluster (z-scores have a
# standard deviation of 1 over all kept zone-years).
SPREAD = {"z_ipm": "Poverty", "z_rural_share": "Rural share", "z_water_coverage": "Piped-water coverage",
          "z_altitude_m": "Altitude"}
zsd = cl.groupby("cluster")[list(SPREAD)].std()
z_c, z_f = zsd.stack().idxmax()                  # (cluster, feature) that varies most
z_c = int(z_c)
text_holds((zsd < 1).all().all() and zsd.stack().max() > 0.9,
           "places more alike within clusters, some only just")

# The check's units, as irca_vs_infant() builds them: one municipality-year, the unweighted mean
# IRCA of its scored zones (in the cluster, or over all of them for the pooled figure).
rows = cl[cl["year"].isin(A.INFANT_YEARS)].dropna(subset=["infant_mortality"])
agg = dict(irca=("irca", "mean"), infant_mortality=("infant_mortality", "first"))
units = rows.groupby(["cluster", "divipola", "year"]).agg(**agg)
pooled_units = rows.groupby(["divipola", "year"]).agg(**agg, zones=("zone", "nunique"))
text_holds(len(pooled_units) == pooled_n, "the pooled units")
one_zone = (pooled_units["zones"] == 1).mean()

# Range: the clusters were formed partly on IRCA, so it varies less inside some of them. A narrow
# range tends to weaken a rank correlation, but the four values do not follow the ranges.
sd_all = pooled_units["irca"].std()
sd_c = units.groupby(level="cluster")["irca"].std()
narrow, wide = [int(c) for c in sd_c.index if sd_c[c] < sd_all], [int(c) for c in sd_c.index if sd_c[c] >= sd_all]
c_flat = int(sd_c.idxmax())                     # where IRCA varies most
text_holds(narrow and wide and c_hi in narrow and (sd_c[narrow] < 0.7 * sd_all).all()
           and rho["spearman_rho"].abs().idxmin() == c_flat, "IRCA's spread within the clusters")

# Chance: how far ρ could move with another draw of places. Resample municipalities with
# replacement, keeping each one's years together (they are not independent draws), recompute ρ,
# and keep the middle 95% of B draws. A fixed seed makes it the same on every render.
B = 1000
rng = np.random.default_rng(A.SEED)


def interval(d):
    d = d.reset_index()
    groups = list(d.groupby("divipola").indices.values())
    draws = []
    for _ in range(B):
        pick = rng.integers(0, len(groups), len(groups))
        s = d.iloc[np.concatenate([groups[i] for i in pick])]
        draws.append(s["irca"].corr(s["infant_mortality"], method="spearman"))
    return np.percentile(draws, [2.5, 97.5])


ci_all = interval(pooled_units)
ci = {c: interval(units.loc[c]) for c in rho.index}
hw = {c: (hi - lo) / 2 for c, (lo, hi) in ci.items()}
zero_in = [c for c, (lo, hi) in ci.items() if lo < 0 < hi]
steps = np.diff(np.sort(rho["spearman_rho"].to_numpy()))
text_holds(all(np.isclose(units.loc[c].corr(method="spearman").loc["irca", "infant_mortality"],
                          rho.loc[c, "spearman_rho"]) for c in rho.index), "the check's units")
text_holds(ci_all[0] > 0 and min(hw.values()) > steps.max() and c_hi not in zero_in
           and 0 < len(zero_in) < k, "the intervals of @tbl-rho")

# Blank rates: the series has no zeros, so a blank may be a recorded zero.
my = cl[cl["year"].isin(A.INFANT_YEARS)].drop_duplicates(["divipola", "year"])
blank = my["infant_mortality"].isna().mean()
pop = w.raw().groupby(["divipola", "year"])["population"].sum()
my_pop = my.join(pop.rename("muni_pop"), on=["divipola", "year"])
text_holds(w.raw()["infant_mortality"].eq(0).sum() == 0
           and my_pop.loc[my_pop["infant_mortality"].isna(), "muni_pop"].median()
           < my_pop.loc[my_pop["infant_mortality"].notna(), "muni_pop"].median(),
           "a series without zeros, blank in smaller places")


def clusters_text(cs):
    return f"cluster {cs[0]}" if len(cs) == 1 else "clusters " + ", ".join(map(str, cs[:-1])) + f" and {cs[-1]}"


# fig-wat-within's alt text: how far the band medians move within a cluster.
band_move = bins.groupby("cluster")["median"].agg(lambda m: m.max() - m.min()).max()
alt_text_holds(f"{band_move:.1f}" == "3.1" and sgn(rho_lo) == "−0.04" and sgn(rho_hi) == "+0.10",
               "fig-wat-within")
# fig-wat-pooled's alt text: about four thousand points, most at low IRCA, a handful above 100.
high_rates = int((pooled_units["infant_mortality"] > 100).sum())
alt_text_holds(round(pooled_n, -3) == 4000 and (pooled_units["irca"] <= 14).mean() > 0.5
               and 0 < high_rates < 20 and 0 < pooled_rho < 0.2, "fig-wat-pooled")

# Tunja (@sec-tunja-kind) in this check: one municipality-year, the mean IRCA of its zones.
tj = cl[(cl["divipola"] == "15001") & cl["year"].isin(A.INFANT_YEARS)].dropna(subset=["infant_mortality"])
tj_c = int(tj["cluster"].iloc[0])
tj_mean = tj.groupby("year")["irca"].mean()
tj_u = tj[tj["zone"] == "urban"].set_index("year")["irca"]
tj_r = tj[tj["zone"] == "rural"].set_index("year")["irca"]
tj_share = tj["rural_share"].max()
tj_yr = int((tj_r - tj_u).idxmax())             # the year its zones' water differed most
text_holds(tj["municipio"].eq("TUNJA").all() and tj["cluster"].eq(tj_c).all()
           and list(tj_u.index) == list(tj_r.index) == list(tj_mean.index) and (tj_u < tj_r).all(),
           "Tunja's averaged zones")
```

The analysis was built to ask whether places with worse water have worse outcomes, and the
temptation, once there is a chart, is to read the answer as an effect: worse water causes more
infant deaths. The data cannot support that sentence, and this chapter shows why, with the
analysis's own numbers.

One more comparison, the association between water safety and infant mortality *within* each kind
of place, comes out weak in every kind, and in one as large as across all of them. But neither a
strong association nor a weak one could settle the causal question here, and the reasons decide how
the results must be written. That last part is not a formality: the sentence a reader quotes is the
one you publish.

::: opener
- Explain what Spearman's ρ measures, and read it across all places and within each kind.
- Explain why comparing within a cluster holds poverty, rurality and coverage only partly fixed, and
  why the four values cannot be ranked.
- Name the paths that can create or hide an association here, and say which way each could push.
- Write a result with verbs of association, the rows compared, its limits and what it does not show.

: your `water-quality` folder at checkpoint 08, with named clusters on the clusters page.

  per cluster and a sentence saying the check is descriptive.

## Worse water, more infant deaths? {#sec-water-within}

The measure is *Spearman's* $\rho$ (rho), which asks whether two variables rise and fall together in
rank order: sort the places by each variable, and see whether the two orders agree. It runs from −1
(perfectly opposite) through 0 to +1 (perfectly together), where 0 means no *monotonic* relation, one
in which a variable tends to rise as the other rises, though not necessarily along a straight line.
Because it uses ranks, it is not thrown by extreme values, which matters with small municipalities'
noisy rates.

Across all municipality-years with both values in `{python} IM_YEARS`, $\rho$ between utility-supplied
IRCA and infant mortality is `{python} sgn(pooled_rho)` (n = `{python} w.fmt(pooled_n)`, the number of
municipality-years compared). @fig-wat-pooled shows what so weak an association looks like: a cloud
with no visible slope.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-pooled
#| fig-cap: "Every municipality-year with both values, 2017–2019 and 2021–2023: utility-supplied IRCA, the mean of its scored zones, against infant mortality (log scale). Descriptive only."
#| fig-alt: "A dense cloud of about four thousand points, one per municipality-year, with utility-supplied IRCA from 0 to 100 across and infant mortality on a log scale up. Most points sit at low IRCA, the cloud shows no clear slope, and a handful of rates rise above 100 per 1,000. The printed Spearman correlation is weak and positive."
#| classes: on-light
with style():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize(7.0, 3.4))
    ax.scatter(pooled_units["irca"], pooled_units["infant_mortality"], s=6, alpha=0.25, color=ACCENT,
               linewidths=0)
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(FixedLocator([2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200]))
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ScalarFormatter())
    ax.yaxis.set_minor_locator(FixedLocator([]))
    ax.set_xlim(-2, 102)
    ax.set_xlabel("Utility-supplied IRCA (0–100)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Infant mortality\nper 1,000")
    ax.text(0.98, 0.95, f"ρ = {sgn(pooled_rho)}\nn = {w.fmt(pooled_n)}", transform=ax.transAxes,
            ha="right", va="top", color=INK)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

A small positive association across all places could come from water, or from everything that
differs between places with safe and unsafe water. The clusters offer a partial *control*, a way of
comparing like with like: within a cluster, places are more alike in poverty, rurality, coverage and
altitude than across the country, though far from equal (@tbl-within-spread).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-within-spread
#| tbl-cap: "How much four features still vary inside each cluster: the standard deviation of their z-scores, against 1 across all kept zone-years."
#| output: asis
print("| Feature | " + " | ".join(str(c) for c in zsd.index) + " |")
print("|---|" + "--:|" * len(zsd.index))
for col, label in SPREAD.items():
    print(f"| {label} | " + " | ".join(f"{zsd.loc[c, col]:.2f}" for c in zsd.index) + " |")
```

Every value is below 1, but some only just: inside cluster `{python} z_c`,
`{python} SPREAD[z_f].lower()` varies almost as much as across all kept zone-years. So the check
repeats the comparison inside each cluster (@fig-wat-within), where some of the differences between
places are smaller.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-within
#| fig-cap: "Median infant mortality by utility-supplied IRCA band, within each cluster; 2017–2019 and 2021–2023 pooled. Bands with fewer than 20 municipality-years are not drawn. Descriptive only."
#| fig-alt: "Four small panels, one per cluster, each titled with the cluster's number and kind. Each shows median infant mortality across the IRCA risk bands, labelled N, L, M, H and U for no risk, low, medium, high and unfit. Within any cluster the medians differ across the bands by at most 3.1 per 1,000, and the Spearman correlations printed on the panels lie between −0.04 and +0.10."
#| classes: on-light
nr, nc = grid(k)
small = nr == 1                                 # the HTML edition's panels in a row
fs = 8 if small else 10
with style():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nr, nc, figsize=figsize(7.2, 2.9, rows=nr), sharey=True, squeeze=False)
    for i, (ax, (c, g)) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, bins.groupby("cluster"))):
        pos = [A.IRCA_BANDS.index(b) for b in g["irca_band"]]
        ax.plot(pos, g["median"], marker=A.CLUSTER_MARKERS[c - 1], ms=5, color=colors[c])
        ax.set_title(textwrap.fill(f"{c} · {kind[c]}", 16 if small else 20, break_on_hyphens=False),
                     fontsize=fs, loc="left", fontweight="bold", color=colors[c])
        ax.text(0.05, 0.06, f"ρ = {sgn(rho.loc[c, 'spearman_rho'])}\nn = {rho.loc[c, 'n']:,}",
                transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=fs, color=INK)
        ax.set_xticks(range(5), ["N", "L", "M", "H", "U"], fontsize=fs)
        ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=fs)
        if i % nc == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel("Infant mortality\nper 1,000", fontsize=fs)
    axes.flat[0].set_ylim(0, bins["median"].max() * 1.3)
    fig.supxlabel("IRCA band: N no risk · L low · M medium · H high · U unfit"
                  if small else "IRCA band: N no risk · L low · M medium\nH high · U unfit", fontsize=fs)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

Within the clusters, $\rho$ runs from `{python} sgn(rho_lo)` in cluster `{python} c_lo` to
`{python} sgn(rho_hi)` in cluster `{python} c_hi`, where it is as large as across all places
(@tbl-rho). These figures cannot be ranked against each other, or set beside the pooled one, at face
value, for three reasons.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rho
#| tbl-cap: "Spearman's ρ between utility-supplied IRCA and infant mortality, with its 95% interval and the spread of IRCA, over all places and within each cluster. One row: a municipality-year."
#| output: asis
print("| | n | ρ | 95% interval | SD of IRCA |")
print("|---|--:|--:|:-:|--:|")


def ci_text(lo, hi):
    return f"{sgn(lo)} to {sgn(hi)}"


print(f"| All places | {w.fmt(pooled_n)} | {sgn(pooled_rho)} | {ci_text(*ci_all)} | {sd_all:.1f} |")
for c in rho.index:
    print(f"| Cluster {c} | {w.fmt(int(rho.loc[c, 'n']))} | {sgn(rho.loc[c, 'spearman_rho'])} "
          f"| {ci_text(*ci[c])} | {sd_c[c]:.1f} |")
```

The first is range. The clusters were formed partly on IRCA, so inside `{python} clusters_text(narrow)`
it varies far less than across all places, and inside `{python} clusters_text(wide)` more. A narrower
range tends to weaken a rank correlation, but that does not explain these four: $\rho$ is largest in
cluster `{python} c_hi`, where IRCA varies little, and closest to zero in cluster `{python} c_flat`,
where it varies most.

The second is chance. To see how far $\rho$ could move with another draw of places, the book redraws
each set's municipalities `{python} w.fmt(B)` times, with replacement and keeping each municipality's
years together, and recomputes $\rho$ every time; the middle 95% of those values is the interval in
@tbl-rho. Each cluster's interval reaches `{python} f"{min(hw.values()):.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{max(hw.values()):.2f}"` either side of its $\rho$, more than the gaps between neighbouring
values, so these data cannot rank the four. The intervals for `{python} clusters_text(zero_in)` include
zero; the pooled one does not.

The third is the unit, because the unit follows the outcome. Infant mortality is measured for a whole
municipality, so each municipality-year counts once, with the mean IRCA of its zones: all of them for
the pooled figure, only those in the cluster for a cluster's. That mean is unweighted, and it covers
only the zones with a score: in `{python} f"{one_zone:.0%}"` of the pooled municipality-years only one
zone has one. So the IRCA beside a rate is one zone's score or the plain mean of two, not what the
average resident drinks.

It would be easy to read this as "water does not matter". That reading is as unsupported as the first one.

::: think
Within cluster `{python} c_flat`, $\rho$ is close to zero. Write the sentence a councillor might wrongly
take from it, and an honest one.

Wrong: "In `{python} kind[c_flat].lower()` places, water quality makes no difference to infant deaths."
Honest: "Within the `{python} kind[c_flat].lower()` kind, municipality-years with higher utility-supplied
IRCA did not have markedly higher recorded infant mortality (`{python} IM_YEARS`). This does not show
that water has no effect: under-reporting, blank rates and the mismatch between zone and municipality
could hide one."
:::

## What else could explain it {#sec-confounders}

@fig-confounders draws the paths between water and infant mortality that the data cannot separate.

![What else could explain it. The dashed arrow is the question; every other path can create an association without an effect, or hide an effect that exists.](../media/diagrams/confounders){#fig-confounders .on-light fig-alt="The question is whether unsafe water raises infant mortality, a dashed arrow from water safety to infant deaths. Other paths connect the two. Poverty and rurality make water less safe and also make infant deaths more likely, a confounder. Poverty also limits health-service access, which affects infant deaths, and weakens reporting quality, which stands between real and recorded deaths: weak registration hides deaths, and blank rates are left out of the data. And IRCA is measured per zone while infant deaths are per municipality, so a pattern across places need not hold for the people in them."}

**Poverty and rurality** are likely *confounders*. A confounder is a third variable that affects both
the exposure, here water safety, and the outcome, here infant deaths, so the two move together even if
one has no effect on the other. Poorer, more rural places tend to have less safe water and, for other
reasons, more infant deaths, so they can produce an association between water and mortality with no
effect of water at all. **Health-service access** carries part of that path: poorer and remoter places
have less of it, and less access means more infant deaths.

**Reporting quality** is a problem of measurement, and it works the other way: places with weak birth
and death registration record fewer infant deaths than occur, and if those are also the places with
unsafe water, under-recording can *hide* a real effect. Blanks add a second problem. The series holds
no zeros, so a blank rate may mean no deaths were recorded, and `{python} f"{blank:.0%}"` of the
clustered municipality-years in these years are blank. Leaving them out drops what may be recorded
zeros, which raises small places' averages most: a selection on the outcome itself (@sec-outcomes).

Then there is the **ecological level**. IRCA is measured for an urban or rural zone, infant mortality for
the whole municipality. A pattern across places need not hold for the people in them: the infants who
died need not be the ones drinking the worst water. Drawing individual conclusions from aggregate data is
known as the *ecological fallacy*.

Tunja shows the mismatch in one place. In this check each of its `{python} NUM[len(tj_mean)]`
municipality-years counts once in cluster `{python} tj_c`, with the mean IRCA of its two zones: in
`{python} tj_yr`, for example, `{python} f"{tj_mean[tj_yr]:.2f}"`, halfway between its urban water's
`{python} f"{tj_u[tj_yr]:.1f}"` and its rural water's `{python} f"{tj_r[tj_yr]:.1f}"`, a value neither zone
had. The mean weighs the two zones equally, though at most `{python} f"{tj_share:.0%}"` of Tunja's people
live in the rural one, and the infant mortality beside it is the whole municipality's.

The clusters narrow some of these differences without removing them: within a cluster, places still
differ in poverty and access (@tbl-within-spread). And small municipalities produce extreme rates, which
add noise that flattens any line.

::: think
Pick one of these paths. Could it hide a real effect, or create a fake one?

Poverty can create a fake one: if poorer places tend to have both less safe water and, for other reasons,
more infant deaths, the two move together without water doing anything. Reporting quality can hide a real
one: if unsafe-water places under-record deaths, their measured rates are too low, and a real effect looks
smaller than it is. Only the first is a confounder; the second is a problem of measurement. Each path
pushes one way, but several act at once and their sizes are unknown, so the net bias could go either way,
which is why a correlation cannot settle the question.
:::

@tbl-problems sorts the paths by the kind of problem each one is.

| Problem | Here | Can create a false link? | Can hide a real one? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Confounding | poverty, rurality, health-service access | yes | yes |
| Measurement | weak registration of deaths | yes | yes |
| Selection | blank rates left out | yes | yes |
| Level | IRCA per zone, deaths per municipality | yes | yes |
| Noise | small places' extreme rates | no | yes |

: What could explain the association, or hide one, by kind of problem. Which way each pushes depends on how it is linked to water safety. Comparing within clusters narrows only the first, and only in part. {#tbl-problems}

A causal claim needs a design that handles these paths, not a better chart: for example, comparing places
before and after a change in water treatment, against comparable places without the change, a design
known as *difference-in-differences*. That is a different study, with different data; Hernán and Robins,
in Further reading, cover such designs.

## Writing it honestly {#sec-honest-writing}

Every output of this analysis says the same thing in the same words, because the project's rules require
it: comparisons between clusters are descriptive and do not establish a causal effect of water safety.
In practice that means a few habits:

- Describe what was compared, and over which rows: "within each cluster, `{python} IM_YEARS`,
  municipality-years with both values".
- Use verbs of association ("is higher in", "varies with"), not of effect ("raises", "reduces", "leads
  to").
- Name the data's limits beside the result: the utility-supplied IRCA, the method change in infant
  mortality, the zone-versus-municipality mismatch.
- State what the result does *not* show, in one sentence a reader could quote.

::: pitfall
The causal sentence usually arrives in the last step: a slide title, a blog post's headline, a summary
for a council. Ask the assistant to check every title and summary against the project's rules, and read
them yourself. "Utility-supplied water risk (IRCA) and infant mortality in Colombian municipalities" is a fair title; "How
unsafe water kills infants" is not, however strongly you suspect it.
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- Spearman's $\rho$ measures whether two variables rise and fall together in rank order; across all
  places, utility-supplied IRCA and infant mortality are only weakly associated ($\rho$ =
  `{python} sgn(pooled_rho)`).
- Within the clusters, where places are more alike but far from equal, $\rho$ runs from
  `{python} sgn(rho_lo)` to `{python} sgn(rho_hi)`; range, chance and a different unit mean these
  values cannot be ranked or set beside the pooled one at face value.
- Poverty and rurality are likely confounders that can create an association with no effect, while
  weak reporting and blank rates can hide a real one.
- IRCA is measured per zone and infant mortality per municipality, and reading a pattern across places
  as one about the people in them is the ecological fallacy, as Tunja's averaged zones show.
- Neither a strong nor a weak association settles the causal question; that needs a design, such as
  before-and-after comparisons with comparable places.
- Write about association: name the rows compared, use verbs of association, put the limits beside the
  result and say what it does not show.
:::

Check every title and summary against that rule before it goes out. @sec-publish-many takes the
results, and those sentences, to the officials and the council, in every format they need.

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- C. Spearman, "The proof and measurement of association between two things", *The American Journal of
  Psychology* 15(1) (1904), doi:[10.2307/1412159](https://doi.org/10.2307/1412159), where the rank
  correlation was introduced; cited in `examples/water/references.bib` and checked against its
  publisher's page (2026-11-01).
- W. S. Robinson, "Ecological correlations and the behavior of individuals", *American Sociological Review*
  15(3), 351–357 (1950), doi:[10.2307/2087176](https://doi.org/10.2307/2087176), the classic account of the
  ecological fallacy; cited in `examples/water/references.bib` and checked against its publisher's page
  (2026-11-01; pages from the paper's 2009 reprint in the *International Journal of Epidemiology*, checked
  2026-11-12).
- Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, [*Causal Inference: What If*](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)
  (Boca Raton: Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2020; free online), on confounding and designs for causal questions (checked 2026-11-12).
- SciPy, [`spearmanr`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.spearmanr.html),
  the rank correlation and its assumptions (checked 2026-11-12).
